text.title: Agent Eval Cost Budget Policy Core Rules
text.summary: 6 testable rules every application of agent-eval-cost-budget-policy enforces. Each rule has a statement, a rationale anchored to industry practice, and a source citation.

rule.statement: Nightly cadence runs the full suite; per-PR cadence runs a fast subset ≤20% of full suite by cost.
rule.rationale: Full suite per PR is unaffordable; ≤20% subset catches the common regressions while keeping PR feedback under 10 minutes.

rule.statement: Fast subset is stratified-sampled across capability tags; not random.
rule.rationale: Random sampling over-represents common cases; stratified captures rare-but-load-bearing categories.

rule.statement: Weekly adversarial cadence runs red-team / jailbreak / OOD prompts; separate budget line.
rule.rationale: Mixing adversarial in nightly inflates baseline cost and hides regressions; weekly slot makes the spend visible.

rule.statement: Judge-model fallback: when day's eval spend exceeds 80% of ceiling, switch to a cheaper judge (e.g., Haiku/distilled) until ceiling resets; flag the swap in the report.
rule.rationale: Hard ceiling without fallback halts all evals; cheap fallback degrades signal gracefully.

rule.statement: Policy is versioned at `evals/policy.md` with date + signature; changes require approval.
rule.rationale: Drifting policies make eval cost trends impossible to read.

rule.statement: When monthly eval spend is below $50 or fewer than one PR per day touches the agent, the team MUST NOT split evals into nightly / per-PR / weekly-adversarial cadences, and MUST NOT wire a stratified fast subset or a judge-model fallback. The full suite runs on a single cadence (per-PR if it finishes under 10 minutes, otherwise nightly), and the month's eval spend is recorded with its date so the $50 threshold can be re-checked; the tree is re-entered the first month spend crosses $50 or PR rate reaches one per day.

rationale.source: Beck, Extreme Programming Explained (YAGNI); the methodology's own Applies-If thresholds

rule.rationale: A three-cadence policy costs an engineer-day to author and a policy file to keep in sync; below $50 a month the entire eval bill is smaller than that maintenance, and a fast subset that trims a $1.50 nightly run buys nothing while adding a sampling step that can hide a regression. Recording the spend is what keeps the skip from becoming permanent.
